title: Mildred never got her due; recording standards and the label
summary: Dance says Mildred's due was never paid; Norvo says the stigma gave A&R men an out and Mildred refused sidemen she thought were poor.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Oh, how funny. Oh, gosh. Well listen you know because when I left I left in -- well I went into the Army in '42, you know, and then I came back in '45 and Stanley and I were married right the next year, so -- yeah. It's work- ing -- well we were talking about Mildred, Red, and we sort of jumped ahead a little bit, but it just seemed to me that it's important to talk about Mildred because there aren't the -- there aren't people to talk about Mildred the same way anymore and as you say the myths don't get built up -- you know they get built up over the tragic cases and this and that, you know and -- and I think, you know, I know and you know that she never did get her just dues. And --
I don't she was never -- I don't think she was ever as successful as she could've been, if she hadn't had that stigma about being hard to handle.
Because it was always an out for anybody for anything. You know -- you understand it?
If an A + R man had the date and he didn't like -- he would normally not saying anything. And yet with Mildred he'd chance it. You see what I mean?
Yes. Yes, cause he'd be able to throw the blame somewhere else.

(unintelligible) She tried to keep the level of her recordings high, with good arrangements and all this sort of thing, or good men on the date. Sometimes they didn't want to give it to her. You know what I mean?
They didn't want to pay the money, you mean?
Yeah. Well as you say, not him, not him. They'd have -- they'd want to run in somebody they knew. That didn't go with Mildred.
If they didn't play, they didn't come on the date.
She wouldn't do the date. I respected her.
